title: Drought and erratic rainfall: the risk to crops
text: Drought and erratic rainfall and its impact on farming. Late, short or broken rains cause poor germination, wilting at flowering, and sharp yield loss, especially on sandy low-organic soils.

title: Adapting to drought and erratic rainfall (Guinea savanna)
text: Adapting to drought and erratic rainfall in the Guinea savanna, with one long rainy season and moderately fertile soils. Grow early-maturing drought-tolerant varieties, mulch to conserve moisture, harvest rainwater into basins/zai pits, plant on the first reliable rains, and space to match the season. In the Guinea savanna, time operations to the single rains, top-dress at the onset of steady rainfall, and use the long season for a full-duration variety.

title: Adapting Sorghum to Climate Change
text: Sorghum is a climate-resilient crop cultivated as a staple food in semi-arid regions of Africa and Asia, crucial for food and nutrition security. However, climate change is increasingly impacting sorghum, particularly at the flowering stage when water availability is vital for grain filling, leading to reduced yields. Developing climate-resilient, biotic and abiotic stress-tolerant, market-preferred, and nutrient-dense sorghum varieties is a promising strategy for adaptation. Key technologies for sorghum improvement include mass selection, single seed descent, pure line selection, and marker-assisted selection, enhanced by backcrossing and molecular marker genotyping. Recent advancements such as machine learning algorithms, gene editing, genomic selection, and high-throughput phenotyping tools have improved the precision and speed of crop variety development. Additionally, enhancing genetic diversity to incorporate traits for heat and drought resilience into sorghum breeding pools is essential for future adaptability.

title: Adapting Sorghum Cultivation to Climate Change
text: Sorghum and millet are vital for food security and economic resilience in semi-arid regions, but climate change poses significant challenges to their productivity. To address these challenges, various agronomic adaptation strategies have been introduced. These include conservation tillage, adjusted planting schedules, drought-tolerant crop varieties, and efficient irrigation methods. While many studies have shown the effectiveness of these strategies in reducing climate-related yield losses in staple cereals like maize, rice, and wheat, there is limited research on their benefits for semi-arid crops such as sorghum and millet. This systematic review aims to quantify and synthesize the effects of these adaptation practices on sorghum yields under changing climatic conditions. The insights gained from this synthesis will help identify the most suitable practices for different regions and crop types, ultimately supporting sustainable agricultural management, enhancing future food security, and promoting economic development.

title: Drought Tolerance in Sorghum Landraces
text: Water is crucial for plant growth, and drought significantly impacts crop yields. Sorghum, known for its drought tolerance, was evaluated in a study involving 239 global landraces under simulated drought conditions using polyethylene glycol (PEG) in 2020 and 2024. The study measured drought tolerance through the seedling tolerance coefficient (STC). Results indicated that while more accessions produced more roots under 10% PEG, at 20% PEG, longer roots were more prevalent, showcasing adaptability to drought stress. However, shoot growth was adversely affected across all accessions in both years. A genome-wide association study (GWAS) identified 22 loci related to growth and STC traits, with 19 linked to STC of shoot weight. Notably, 11 loci were found to overlap with previously identified drought-related quantitative trait loci (QTLs). Additionally, 19 candidate genes were identified, with five showing specific expression in roots, highlighting their potential role in enhancing drought tolerance in sorghum.

title: Enhancing Drought Tolerance in Sorghum
text: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) serves as a vital food staple for millions in Sub-Saharan Africa and Asia, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions. While sorghum is known for its drought tolerance, severe drought stress can lead to significant crop loss and reduced productivity. To address this challenge, the development of high-yielding and drought-adapted genotypes is essential for sustainable sorghum production. A study evaluated 225 African sorghum genotypes under various drought stress conditions, including non-stressed, pre-anthesis drought stress, and post-anthesis drought stress. The analysis identified genotypes such as G09 and G109 as best suited for non-stressed environments, while G114 and G56 performed well under both stressed and non-stressed conditions. Additionally, G72 and G75 excelled specifically in pre-anthesis drought stress. This research highlights the importance of selecting and breeding drought-adapted sorghum genotypes to enhance resilience and ensure food security in drought-prone areas.

title: Enhancing Drought Tolerance in Sorghum
text: Sorghum is a vital cereal crop known for its resilience in arid and semiarid environments. However, drought stress poses a significant challenge to its productivity, necessitating the enhancement of drought tolerance traits. One important trait is transpiration efficiency (TE), which indicates a plant's ability to utilize water efficiently. A study involving 182 Ethiopian sorghum accessions revealed substantial genetic variation in TE and related traits, with Durra races showing the highest TE levels. Intermediate races exhibited moderate TE, while several other races demonstrated the lowest efficiency. Strong correlations were established between TE and traits such as total shoot fresh weight, total shoot dry weight, and leaf number. Principal component analysis highlighted key traits influencing TE, while cluster analysis categorized accessions into four distinct groups, with the highest TE found in Cluster IV. These findings underscore the potential of TE in breeding water-efficient sorghum varieties, providing valuable genetic resources for improving drought tolerance in this essential crop.

title: Improving Sorghum Germination through Hydro-Priming in Mali
text: Agriculture in Mali is highly vulnerable to climate change, particularly due to its reliance on rainfall and low adaptive capacity. Early-season droughts can severely limit crop germination and growth, affecting yields in rain-fed agriculture. A promising technique to enhance the germination and establishment of sorghum, a staple crop, is hydro-priming. This method involves soaking seeds in various water sources, such as well and river water, for different durations. Research conducted in 2014 and 2015 demonstrated that hydro-priming significantly improved several germination metrics, including final germination percentage and seedling development, with well and river water yielding the highest germination rates at 85%. Hydro-priming not only enhances germination rate and uniformity but also contributes to better seedling vigor. Implementing hydro-priming in crop fields could be an effective strategy for managing the impacts of early-season drought on sorghum production in Mali.

title: Opportunities and Constraints in Sorghum Production in Nigeria
text: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor [L.] Moench) plays a vital role in food security and industrial demands in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in Nigeria. Despite its importance, the production and productivity of sorghum in Nigeria remain underdeveloped. A participatory rural appraisal (PRA) study involving 250 farmers across three sorghum-growing zones in northern Nigeria highlighted key socio-economic factors. Most sorghum farmers are male (80%), predominantly aged 21-45 years (75.7%), with a household size of fewer than five members (52.3%). The most commonly cultivated varieties are low-yielding landraces such as Kaura (37.4%) and Fara-fara (29.3%), favored for their grain quality. Farmers prioritize traits like high yield, drought tolerance, and Striga resistance. To enhance sorghum production and economic benefits, the study recommends the development of integrated sorghum technologies that align with farmers' preferences, addressing both current opportunities and constraints in the sector.

title: Management of Banana Xanthomonas Wilt
text: Banana is a crucial staple food for over 100 million Africans, yet it faces significant productivity challenges due to various pests and diseases. One of the most severe threats is Banana Xanthomonas wilt, caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. musacearum, which can completely devastate banana plantations. Additionally, nematodes can lead to losses of up to 50% and heighten the crop's vulnerability to other pests and diseases. To combat these issues, the development of improved banana varieties is essential. Traditional breeding methods are hindered by the sterile nature of bananas and the lack of resistance in Musa germplasm, making progress slow or unfeasible. However, advancements in genetic engineering are showing promise. Transgenic bananas that express sweet pepper Hrap and Pflp genes have exhibited complete resistance to X. campestris pv. musacearum in field trials. Similarly, transgenic plantains with cysteine proteinase inhibitors and synthetic peptides have shown improved resistance to nematodes. These innovations represent a significant step towards enhancing agricultural resilience and food security in Africa.

title: Management Strategies for Rice Blast in Nepal
text: Blast, caused by Pyricularia oryzae, is a significant threat to rice production in Nepal, leading to yield losses of 10-30%. The Himalayan foothills are hotspots for the diversity of the blast fungus, resulting in the emergence of new pathotypes that can overcome resistance in popular rice varieties. In 2022, a neck blast epidemic affected 5,000 hectares of the Hardinath-1 variety, causing nearly total yield loss. Changing climate conditions, particularly during the panicle initiation stage, have made the environment more conducive to neck blast development. To address this issue, integrated management strategies are essential. These include developing durable blast-resistant and climate-resilient rice varieties through molecular markers and genomic tools, forecasting disease emergence, and utilizing modern fungicides and biological control methods. Additionally, adjusting planting times, managing weeds, and optimizing agronomic practices are crucial for effective management of rice blast in Nepal.

title: Managing Fusarium Wilt in Organic Banana Farming
text: Fusarium wilt of bananas, caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense, is a significant global threat to banana production, with no effective fungicides or cultural measures currently available for control. Research indicates that organic agriculture may offer a more resilient approach to managing this disease compared to conventional farming. A study comparing organic and conventional banana plantations in north Queensland, Australia, found that organic soils exhibited higher microbial activity and lower disease symptoms in both bananas and tomatoes. Key indicators of soil health, such as nematode diversity and soil sulphate content, were correlated with pathogen growth and plant health. Organic soils had lower levels of plant-parasitic nematodes and higher microbial indicators, suggesting that enhancing soil health through organic practices could suppress Fusarium wilt. Farmers are encouraged to adopt organic farming systems to improve soil health and potentially reduce the impact of Fusarium wilt on banana crops.

Managing an outbreak in the humid forest zone, where heavy rainfall leaches and acidifies soils and fungal pressure is high: Grow resistant varieties, avoid excess nitrogen, apply fungicide at booting on susceptible crops, and drain intermittently. In the humid forest, correct soil acidity with lime, watch for rapid fungal spread under the canopy, and improve drainage on the heavy leached soils.

title: Understanding Rice Blast Caused by Magnaporthe oryzae
text: Rice blast, caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, leads to significant yield losses primarily through injuries on the necks and leaves of rice plants. The neck injuries are generally more critical than those on the leaves. Research has shown that isolates of M. oryzae from leaves exhibit less aggressiveness compared to those from necks, indicating that there is no specialization in the pathogen population based on the organ infected. This suggests that more aggressive isolates that affect leaves during the vegetative stage are likely to also infect necks, potentially leading to a population shift during disease transmission. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for effective disease management strategies. It is important for farmers and agricultural practitioners to monitor both leaf and neck infections to mitigate the impact of rice blast on crop yields.

title: Management of Rice Blast Disease Using Trichoderma harzianum
text: Rice blast (Pyricularia oryzae Cavara) is a significant disease impacting rice crops in Cambodia and globally. To manage this disease, Trichoderma spp., particularly the strain T. harzianum BTB 022, is utilized as a biological control agent through soil treatment, seed treatment, and foliar application. The combination of T. harzianum with resistant rice varieties offers a sustainable approach to mitigate yield losses and address restrictions on fungicide use. Experiments conducted in 2016 and 2017 at Koktrap and Polors agricultural research stations evaluated the effectiveness of T. harzianum on both susceptible and resistant rice varieties. These experiments followed a randomized complete block design with multiple replications. Leaf blast incidence was monitored at various growth stages, and the area under the leaf blast progress curve (AULBPC) was calculated. Additionally, neck blast incidence was assessed at the dough stage, and grain yield was measured at ripening. This integrated management strategy is essential for effective control of rice blast disease.

title: Management of Rice Blast and Bacterial Leaf Blight
text: Rice blast and bacterial leaf blight (BLB) are significant diseases that threaten rice yields across all growing regions under favorable conditions. A genome-wide association study (GWAS) involving 147 rice accessions identified 23 significant marker-trait associations (MTAs) related to these diseases, corresponding to 107 candidate genes for blast and 210 for BLB. The haplo-pheno analysis revealed eight superior haplotypes for blast, with average SES scores from 0.00 to 1.33, and five superior haplotypes for BLB, with scores ranging from 1.52 cm to 4.86 cm. Notably, haplotypes LOC_OS12G39700-H4 and LOC_Os06g30440-H33 showed the lowest average blast scores, while LOC_Os02g12660-H39 had the lowest average lesion length for BLB. A total of ten accessions for blast and eight for BLB were identified, belonging to aus and indx subpopulations from Bangladesh, Brazil, India, Myanmar, and Pakistan, as well as eight accessions from six countries for BLB resistance.

title: Management of Rice Blast Disease Caused by Magnaporthe oryzae
text: Rice blast disease, caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, leads to significant yield losses in rice production worldwide. A recent study focused on developing a mechanistic simulation model for rice blast using STELLA 9.1 software, based on the EPIRICE model from IRRI. The model integrates leaf and neck blast submodels, utilizing a linear regression equation to establish their relationship. Verification was conducted using data from eight sites, with validation at five locations in the Philippines. Graphical comparisons indicated that simulated and observed leaf blast severity and neck blast incidence curves were similar. Statistical validation employed the Wilcoxon test, Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and equivalence tests. Results showed low RMSE values for leaf blast severity and higher values for neck blast incidence. The Wilcoxon test revealed significant differences in leaf blast severity predictions, achieving 60% accuracy for neck blast predictions. However, the equivalence test indicated only 40% accuracy for both leaf blast severity and neck blast incidence, highlighting the complexities of these pathosystems. Potential leaf blast epidemics were mapped in Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, and the Philippines using projected weather data.

title: Integrated Disease Management for Bacterial Wilt in Tomatoes
text: Bacterial wilt, caused by Ralstonia solanacearum, poses a significant threat to tomato farmers, particularly in tropical regions. A study conducted in Coimbatore district, Tamil Nadu, from 2020 to 2023, revealed the disease's prevalence, especially during the Rabi season in areas like Kinathukadavu and Madukarai. An Integrated Disease Management (IDM) approach was evaluated, which included soil amendments, application of Bacillus subtilis, intercropping with marigold, seedling root dipping in streptocycline, and drenching with copper-based fungicides. The IDM treatment (T6) consistently resulted in the lowest disease incidence, ranging from 2.67% to 4.47%, and achieved the highest yield of 394.50-404.63 q/ha, along with a favorable Benefit: Cost ratio of 3.91-3.63. A strong negative correlation was observed between wilt incidence and yield, indicating that IDM T6 provided the best outcomes. These results highlight the effectiveness and sustainability of Integrated Disease Management in combating bacterial wilt and enhancing tomato production in affected areas.

title: Groundnut Seed Management Success Story
text: Adamu, a groundnut farmer from Maugura village, Masasi, has shared his success story regarding his involvement in TL projects. He learned essential skills such as how to grow groundnut seeds, carry out diagnosis, and store them properly. This year, he has begun planting various seeds to continue his research. The Naliendele Institute provided him with approximately 20 lines of seeds, which he is currently working on. Although these seeds have not yet been named, he has planted them in plots, ranging from plot number one to plot number twenty. Adamu's experience highlights the importance of proper seed management and the potential for research to improve crop yields and farming practices in the region.

title: Revitalizing Groundnut Breeding in Ghana
text: Groundnut production in Ghana faced significant decline in the mid-nineties due to various factors, prominently including the rosette disease. This decline was exacerbated by the absence of a dedicated groundnut breeder for over a decade. In 2015, efforts to revitalize the groundnut breeding program were initiated with the support of the Tropical Legumes Projects. Dr. Roger Kanton, Deputy Director of CSIR-SARI, highlighted the importance of this initiative. Dr. Richard Oteng-Frimpong, a young groundnut breeder, noted that only a few local germplasms were available at the time, which posed challenges for the breeding program's success. The reinitiation of the program aims to address the issues caused by the rosette disease and improve groundnut production in the region, ensuring better resilience and sustainability for farmers.

title: Good Practices for Tomato Cultivation
text: This technical guide on good practices for tomato cultivation was prepared by the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) in partnership with the Department of Agriculture (DoA), Sri Lanka. The aim is to guide farmers on the good practices for safe and sustainable cultivation. By following these practices, farmers can enhance the health of their tomato crops, ensuring better yields and quality. The guide emphasizes the importance of understanding the specific needs of tomato plants and implementing strategies that promote their growth while minimizing environmental impact. Sustainable practices not only contribute to the well-being of the crops but also support the overall health of the farming ecosystem. Farmers are encouraged to adopt these guidelines to improve their cultivation methods and achieve better results in their tomato production.

title: Fertilizer Recommendations for Cereal Crops in Ethiopia
text: To meet the growing global demand for food, it is essential to increase crop yields through efficient fertilizer use. In Ethiopia, plant nutrition research began in the 1960s following a soil survey that revealed widespread nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) deficiencies. Initial recommendations from nationwide trials in the 1970s suggested applying 64 kg N ha−1 and 20 kg P ha−1 for all crops, using di-ammonium phosphate and urea. However, research in the 1980s indicated a more tailored approach, recommending 30–138 kg N ha−1 and 0–50 kg P ha−1 based on specific agro-ecological conditions. Despite these recommendations, only 30–40% of smallholder farmers utilize fertilizers at rates below the recommended levels, averaging 37–40 kg ha−1. This limited use, coupled with high prices and declining crop responses, has resulted in only a 10% increase in cereal yields since the 1980s. To address these challenges, research into the integrated application of inorganic and organic fertilizers has shown promise in improving yields and economic benefits.

title: Targeted Fertilizer Recommendations for Smallholder Farmers in Ethiopia
text: Smallholder farmers in Africa often rely on broad fertilizer recommendations that may not suit local production conditions, leading to poor responses. A randomized control trial conducted in Ethiopia examined the effects of targeted extension advice on fertilizer usage and productivity. The study found that when farmers received tailored recommendations, they were able to align their fertilizer application with the suggested levels. This adjustment resulted in increased productivity and profits. Additionally, the research explored whether pairing targeted advice with agricultural insurance would further encourage fertilizer investment. However, the findings indicated no significant difference in the effectiveness of targeted recommendations when combined with agricultural insurance. This suggests that the risk of crop failure may not be a major barrier to fertilizer adoption in this context, or that farmers do not view agricultural insurance as an effective means of mitigating risk. Overall, targeted fertilizer recommendations can play a crucial role in enhancing agricultural productivity among smallholder farmers.

title: Site-Specific Fertilizer Recommendations for Maize in Sub-Saharan Africa
text: In sub-Saharan Africa, the relationship between nutrient application and maize yield varies significantly due to factors such as soil nutrient supply, moisture, crop management, and germplasm. This variability impacts fertilizer use efficiency and crop productivity. To address this, the Nutrient Expert (NE) decision support system has been developed to provide site-specific fertilizer recommendations. NE was calibrated for major maize agroecological zones in Nigeria, Ethiopia, and Tanzania using data from 735 on-farm nutrient omission trials conducted between 2015 and 2017. Performance trials from 2016 to 2018 evaluated NE recommendations against soil-test based recommendations, blanket fertilizer recommendations, and a control with no fertilizer. Results showed that maize yield response to nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) varied by location, with average responses of 2.4, 1.6, and 0.2 t ha−1 in Nigeria; 2.3, 0.9, and 0.2 t ha−1 in Ethiopia; and 1.5, 0.8, and 0.2 t ha−1 in Tanzania. Secondary and micronutrients also contributed to yield increases in specific areas.

title: Site-Specific Fertilizer Recommendations for Maize in Malawi
text: To address the challenge of low maize productivity in Malawi, it is essential to implement spatially explicit and nutrient-specific fertilizer recommendations that consider soil heterogeneity and economic constraints. Traditional blanket recommendations fail to account for localized variations in soil properties, climate, and nutrient responses, which limits their effectiveness. This study utilized a Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) model to generate fine-scale (250 m resolution) fertilizer recommendations for nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), sulfur (S), and zinc (Zn). The model was trained on 20 features, including nutrient management, soil, climate, topography, and hydrological factors. Results indicated significant spatial variation in nutrient requirements, with nitrogen and phosphorus exhibiting the widest ranges in both agronomic and economic rates. The economic optimum rates were found to be slightly lower than agronomic rates, highlighting the need for tailored nutrient management strategies in smallholder maize systems to enhance productivity effectively.

title: Fertilizer Recommendations for Maize in Semi-Arid Tanzania
text: The Africa RISING program utilizes the mother-baby trial approach to test and validate fertilizer recommendations for maize in semi-arid Tanzania. During the 2013 and 2014 growing seasons, ICRAF and partners developed a fertilizer plan recommending 30 kg P/ha and 60 kg N/ha. Farmers participated in testing these rates on their fields as baby trials after receiving training on promising fertilizer technologies and good agronomic practices (GAP). In 2016, 605 farmers (55% male and 45% female) established baby trials to validate the effectiveness of these fertilizer-maize variety technologies. The fertilizers tested included Minjingu and Yara Mila Cereals, while the maize varieties included Staha, Kilima, SEED Co, and a local variety known as Gunzi Jekundu. Each farmer assessed the performance of improved and local maize varieties with and without the recommended fertilizers, applying them according to guidelines provided by the companies. This approach aims to enhance maize productivity in the region through validated and farmer-driven trials.

title: Refining Fertilizer Recommendations for Maize in Smallholder Landscapes
text: Improving fertilizer recommendations is crucial for enhancing food security among smallholder farmers. Current practices involve blanket recommendations across various agro-ecological zones, which do not account for the spatial variability in fertilizer response (FR) and nutrient use efficiency (N-AE) of maize crops. A study analyzing 71 on-farm publications from Kenya and Sub-Sahara Africa revealed that the average FR was 2, with considerable variation from 1 to 28.5. Notably, 18% of plots in SSA were non-responsive, exhibiting an FR of less than 1. Key factors influencing N-AE in Kenya included P-Olsen, silt content, soil pH, clay, and rainfall, while in SSA, soil pH, exchangeable K, and texture were significant. However, available data on soil, climate, and management factors only explained less than 33% of the variation in FR and N-AE. Therefore, refining fertilizer recommendations should incorporate detailed information on soil types and properties to enhance nutrient management for maize cultivation.

title: Enhancing Maize Productivity in Northern Ghana
text: In northern Ghana, smallholder farmers face challenges such as low soil fertility and unpredictable rainfall, leading to low productivity. A study evaluated the effectiveness of site-specific fertilizer recommendations (SSF) combined with maize-cowpea intercropping to enhance productivity and resilience. Demonstrations were conducted in ten communities across the Northern and Upper West regions. Two treatments were assessed: maize-cowpea intercrop with SSF and sole maize with farmer-applied fertilizer rates. Despite a long dry spell in 2024 affecting many crops, the SSF + intercrop plots yielded significantly higher maize grain at 4,078 kg ha-1 compared to the farmer practice of 2,826 kg ha-1, demonstrating resilience against drought. Average yields from farmer-replicated plots reached 3,124 kg ha-1, surpassing the regional average of 1,600 kg ha-1. This study indicates that tailored fertilizer recommendations alongside maize-cowpea intercropping can contribute to sustainable production, bridging yield gaps, and improving food security in the Guinea savannah agroecological zone.

title: Tailored Fertilizer Recommendations for Maize in Ghana
text: Agroadvisory services are crucial for enhancing sustainable agricultural practices, especially in regions like Ghana that face climate fluctuations and resource limitations. The Alliance of Bioversity International & CIAT, in collaboration with IITA and CSIR, is working to integrate input supply, insurance, and advisory services to support maize farmers. This initiative focuses on improving fertilizer use recommendations based on specific soil tests and experimental datasets. Utilizing the AgWise framework, the project has generated site-specific fertilizer recommendations by analyzing over 1,740 data points from scientific publications, field trials, and crop cut surveys. The modeling process included a thorough exploration of soil characteristics, climate patterns, and topography, resulting in a dataset of 1,532 observations across 47 data columns. The H2O package within RStudio was employed for model training, ensuring that the recommendations are precise and tailored to the unique conditions of the Guinea Savannah zone, ultimately aiming to enhance maize productivity and mitigate associated risks.

title: Next-Generation Decision Support Tool for Fertilizer Recommendations in Maize
text: This study evaluates the potential of a Next-Generation Decision Support Tool (DST) designed to provide data-driven, season-tailored, site-specific fertilizer recommendations (SSRs) to improve maize performance in Ethiopia. The DST utilizes a national maize yield response to fertilizer database, geo-referenced soil profiles, spatial covariates, and a Random Forest algorithm to optimize nitrogen-phosphorus (N-P) rates at a resolution of 250 m. During the 2024 season, the tool's effectiveness was validated through on-farm trials on 59 fields across Meskan, Mareko, and Shala districts, comparing DST-based SSR with district-level local recommendations and farmers' current practices. Results indicated that grain yield was significantly influenced by both location and fertilizer strategy, with SSR consistently outperforming local recommendations and often farmers' practices, particularly in Mareko and Shala. Economic analyses revealed clear profitability advantages of SSR over local recommendations across all districts, highlighting the tool's potential to enhance maize production through tailored nutrient management.

title: Impact of Site-Specific Nutrient Management Recommendations on Maize Production
text: In Sub-Saharan Africa, agricultural extension has struggled to enhance technology adoption and productivity growth among farmers. A study conducted in northern Nigeria focused on the effectiveness of site-specific nutrient management recommendations for maize production. The research involved a randomized controlled trial with smallholder farmers, analyzing the impact of two extension treatments: recommendations with and without additional information on output price variability and expected returns. The findings revealed that site-specific recommendations improved fertilizer management practices and maize yields, although they did not significantly increase overall fertilizer use. Notably, recommendations that included information on expected returns led to greater fertilizer investments that continued beyond the initial year. However, the overall increases in investments and net revenues were modest, indicating that while targeted advice can enhance practices, the effects on productivity and investment levels remain incremental over the treatment period.

title: Optimal Fertilizer Application for Maize in Ethiopia
text: The use of fertilizers in balanced and adequate amounts is essential for enhancing maize productivity. In Ethiopia, unbalanced nutrient management has been a significant factor in low maize yields, primarily due to insufficient information on nutrient dose-responses across different soil types. A study conducted from 2014 to 2017 on 29 farmers' fields in Oromia and the Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples Region (SNNPR) aimed to quantify maize yield response to varying application rates of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and sulphur (S). The agronomic optimum rates were determined to be 46 kg N, 40 kg P, 17 kg K, and 10 kg S per hectare on Nitisols, while on Andosols, the optimum rates were 184 kg N, 20 kg P, and 30 kg S per hectare. The predicted maximum yields with balanced nutrient application were higher on Nitisols (4630–6094 kg ha−1) compared to Andosols (3397–3640 kg ha−1). Proper nutrient management is crucial for achieving optimal maize yields.

title: Optimizing Nitrogen Management in Cereal Production
text: Recent geopolitical conflicts and supply disruptions have highlighted vulnerabilities in the global fuel-fertilizer-food nexus, particularly concerning nitrogen (N) fertilizer price spikes that threaten food security. To maintain staple cereal yields, differentiated responses are essential for both over- and under-fertilized agricultural systems. Integrated management of organic and inorganic N sources can lead to significant N-fertilizer savings—estimated at 11% in India, 49% in Ethiopia, and 44% in Malawi. Transitioning to more cost-effective high-N fertilizers, such as urea, in conjunction with compost and legumes, can enhance N optimization in N-deficient systems. Additionally, targeted and efficient N-fertilizer use will benefit systems with surplus N. It is crucial to implement geospatially differentiated fertilization strategies that prioritize high-N fertilizer supply to low-yield, N-deficient areas while ensuring balanced fertilization of N, P, K, and micronutrients in high-yield systems. Governments should consider investing in extension services and realigning subsidies to promote improved N management at the farm level.

title: Micronutrient Deficiencies in Sub-Saharan Africa Soils
text: A synthesis of agronomic datasets and scientific literature reveals widespread micronutrient deficiencies in arable soils of sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Zinc (Zn) is the most prevalent deficiency, followed by boron (B), iron (Fe), molybdenum (Mo), and copper (Cu). The co-occurrence of multiple micronutrient deficiencies is common, impacting the nutritional quality of key food crops such as maize, beans, wheat, and rice. Micronutrient fertilization and agronomic biofortification can enhance micronutrient concentrations in edible plant parts, proving profitable in 60–80% of cases. However, variations in plant nutritional quality and profitability are significant, influenced by factors such as crop species, fertilizer types, application methods, climate, initial soil conditions, and soil chemistry. To improve micronutrient use efficiency, it is essential to adapt fertilizer rates and types to specific soil and management conditions. This approach can help address the micronutrient deficiencies affecting crop yields and nutritional quality in SSA.

title: Understanding Fall Armyworm Impact on Maize and Rice
text: Fall Armyworm (FAW), Spodoptera frugiperda, is a significant pest affecting over 350 plant species, including maize and rice. Research indicates that the developmental period from egg to adult is longer when FAW feeds on rice compared to maize, extending larval development by 15.15%. FAW larvae reared on maize exhibit higher weights than those on rice, although pupal weights are similar across both crops. Notably, female FAW adults emerge before males, with females from maize appearing 3.36 days earlier. Additionally, females from rice have longer pre-oviposition periods and shorter oviposition periods than those from maize. The age-specific fecundity rate peaks at 40 days for rice and 33 days for maize. Feeding on maize enhances reproduction rates, with the intrinsic rate of natural increase (rm) rising from 0.121 on rice to 0.173 on maize. Consequently, FAW feeding on rice leads to longer generation lengths and doubling times, highlighting the importance of effective pest management strategies in maize cultivation.

title: Controlling Maize Stem Borer on Maize (Guinea savanna)
text: Maize Stem Borer (Busseola fusca / Chilo partellus), a pest of maize. title: Identifying and Managing Fall Armyworm in Maize
text: Spodoptera frugiperda, commonly known as fall armyworm (FAW), was first reported in Uganda in 2016 and has become a significant pest for maize farmers. A survey of 1,289 maize farmers revealed that 85% ranked FAW as their top pest problem. By 2018, over 90% of farmers had encountered FAW, with about 80% observing it in their fields. Common symptoms of FAW damage included windowing, near tunnel damage, and holes on cobs. Farmers identified various developmental stages of FAW, including eggs (10%), young larvae (78.7%), mature larvae (73.5%), and adult moths (6.7%). While insecticides were the primary control method, some farmers also utilized plant extracts, hand-picking, sand, and ash. Information on FAW was sourced from fellow farmers, radio/TV, extension agents, input dealers, print media, research, and NGOs. There is a pressing need for clear and uniform information to aid farmers in effectively managing this pest.

title: Effective Management of Striga hermonthica in Maize Production
text: Striga hermonthica, commonly known as purple witchweed, poses a significant challenge to maize production in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in areas with poor soil conditions. A study conducted in western Kenya evaluated various management strategies for controlling S. hermonthica, including intercropping maize with legumes such as peanut, soybean, and silverleaf desmodium, as well as growing maize as a sole crop. Results indicated that maize grown in rotation with soybean yielded the highest grain output of 3,672 kg ha−1 under artificial infestation. Under natural infestation, the highest yields were observed with silverleaf desmodium and peanut cropping systems, yielding 3,203 kg ha−1 and 3,193 kg ha−1, respectively. The use of herbicide-resistant and Striga spp.-resistant maize varieties, particularly when intercropped with legumes, proved to be a more effective control method than using individual technologies. Additionally, fewer S. hermonthica plants emerged in maize grown with silverleaf desmodium, highlighting its potential in integrated pest management strategies.

title: Effective Control of Striga hermonthica in Maize Using Herbicide Coated Seeds
text: The use of small doses of imazapyr and pyrithiobac for seed coatings of imazapyr-resistant maize hybrids (IR-Maize) has proven effective in controlling Striga hermonthica. Field trials conducted in Bauchi and Kano States of Nigeria during 2014 and 2015, under heavy Striga infestation, demonstrated that herbicide-coated seeds significantly reduced the number of emerged Striga per square meter and the associated damage symptoms in farmers' fields. In Kano, herbicide-treated hybrids showed a reduction of 4.9 to 7.9 times fewer emerged Striga compared to untreated hybrids. Similarly, in Bauchi, untreated IR-maize hybrids had over four times more emerged Striga than the treated hybrids. The Striga-resistant open pollinated variety (OPV) had significantly higher Striga counts than the treated hybrids. While the herbicide seed coating effectively reduced Striga infestation, the impact on grain yields was inconsistent due to strong seasonal effects. Overall, coating IR-maize seeds with imazapyr is an effective strategy for managing Striga in maize cultivation.

title: Impact of Weevil on Local vs Improved Plantain Varieties
text: In the humid forest of Cameroon, local cultivars of plantain are significantly affected by weevil infestations, with severity levels reaching 55.0 ± 5.2%. In contrast, improved plantain hybrids exhibit much lower weevil severity, ranging from 21.0 ± 4.6% to 28.5 ± 3.2%. This disparity highlights the vulnerability of local varieties to pest damage compared to their improved counterparts. The study evaluated eight genotypes, including seven improved and one local variety, over two growing cycles. The findings indicate that the improved hybrids not only show better resistance to pests but also perform better in terms of agronomic traits, such as higher average bunch weight. These results suggest that adopting improved plantain varieties could enhance production and reduce losses due to weevil infestations, ultimately contributing to food security and income generation in the region.

title: Impact of Cowpea Aphids on Crop Yield
text: Cowpea aphids (Aphis craccivora Koch) are a significant pest affecting cowpea crops by causing direct damage and acting as vectors for viruses. The economic yield of cowpea is threatened by these pests, necessitating research into resistance mechanisms. A study involving 365 cowpea mini-core accessions was conducted to identify genetic loci associated with resistance to aphids from Kano, Nigeria. Accessions were inoculated with A. craccivora in controlled environments, and damage severity was evaluated after 21 days. The results showed significant phenotypic variation among accessions, indicating the influence of major genes on resistance. A genome-wide scan revealed three major genomic regions on chromosomes Vu10, Vu08, and Vu02, along with two minor regions on Vu01 and Vu06, linked to aphid resistance. Key genes identified, such as Vigun01g233100.1 and Vigun02g088900.1, are involved in stress responses and insect feeding. These findings are crucial for developing marker-assisted breeding strategies aimed at enhancing durable resistance to cowpea aphids.

title: Integrated Pest Management for Cowpea Production
text: Cowpea is a vital grain legume that provides essential protein for rural families in Sub-Saharan Africa and nutritious fodder for livestock. However, its production is severely threatened by field and storage insect pests, which can lead to losses of up to 100%. While synthetic pesticides have been used for pest control, their negative impacts on health and the environment highlight the urgent need for integrated pest management (IPM) alternatives. Recent advancements in West Africa have focused on developing IPM strategies that include host plant resistance, biological control, biopesticides, and good cultural practices. These innovations have been tested and validated by research institutions and disseminated through farmer field schools, field demonstrations, and community education. By adopting these environmentally safer and scalable IPM options, cowpea stakeholders can minimize pest problems, reduce reliance on harmful pesticides, and ensure the sustainability of cowpea production, ultimately contributing to food security in the region.

title: Effective Control Strategies for Fall Armyworm in Maize
text: The fall armyworm, Spodoptera frugiperda, has emerged as a significant pest affecting maize fields across sub-Saharan Africa. Its rapid spread necessitates effective integrated pest management strategies, which rely heavily on efficient monitoring and surveillance. Recent studies indicate that the commercially available Unitrap is the most effective trap design for capturing fall armyworm. In contrast, a homemade 2 L jar trap, while inexpensive, collected significantly fewer fall armyworms, especially during periods of low pest density. Additionally, the choice of pheromone blend is crucial; a 4-component blend consistently attracted the highest numbers of fall armyworm across various conditions. These findings underscore the importance of selecting appropriate trapping methods and pheromone lures to mitigate fall armyworm infestations in smallholder maize farms. Implementing these strategies can enhance pest management efforts and support sustainable agricultural practices.

title: Mitigation Strategies for Fall Armyworm in Maize Production
text: This study investigates the factors influencing the adoption and effectiveness of fall armyworm (FAW) mitigation strategies among maize farmers in Burundi. FAW poses a significant threat to maize production and food security, yet there is limited understanding of what drives farmers to adopt control measures and their subsequent impact on yields. An analysis of data from 536 maize farmers across five provinces revealed that approximately 68% adopted FAW mitigation methods, primarily relying on chemical control. Socio-economic factors, access to information, credit, and extension services positively influenced both adoption and the intensity of use. Notably, farmers who adopted these strategies achieved significantly higher maize yields compared to non-adopters. The findings highlight that while FAW mitigation strategies can enhance maize yields, the reliance on chemical methods indicates a limited uptake of integrated pest management practices. Recommendations include strengthening extension services, promoting Integrated Pest Management training, improving access to credit, and enhancing rural infrastructure to support sustainable FAW control.

title: Identifying Fall Armyworm in Maize Fields
text: The fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) poses a significant threat to maize production in Africa, with outbreaks first reported in 2016. Field surveys in Benin and Mali indicate that fall armyworm eggs and neonates can be found approximately one week after maize plants emerge. However, scouting for these pests is challenging and time-consuming. Research suggests that the timing of oviposition by female fall armyworms can be predicted. By analyzing data from young maize seedlings, it was estimated that around 210 accumulated Degree Days (DD) are necessary for the early detection of neonate larvae. This information is crucial for timely pest detection and can assist farmers in implementing effective control measures. Understanding the life cycle and timing of fall armyworm can help mitigate yield losses and improve maize production outcomes.

title: Identification of Fall Armyworm in Maize
text: The fall armyworm, scientifically known as Spodoptera frugiperda, is a significant noctuid pest primarily affecting maize on the American continents. Despite being intercepted occasionally by European quarantine services, it has recently emerged as an invasive species in West and Central Africa, with outbreaks first recorded in early 2016. Genetic analysis of samples collected from maize in Nigeria and São Tome indicates the presence of at least two distinct haplotypes, suggesting that there have been multiple introductions of this pest into Africa. The emergence of the fall armyworm poses a new threat to maize crops in tropical Africa, necessitating urgent attention and management strategies to mitigate its impact on agricultural production in the region.

title: Effective Management of Fall Armyworm in Lebanese Maize Fields
text: The invasive pest, fall armyworm (FAW), Spodoptera frugiperda, poses a significant threat to irrigated summer maize production in Lebanon, impacting food security and farmers' income. A field study conducted in Qob Elias, Bekaa valley during the summer of 2024 evaluated the effectiveness of insecticides based on pheromone traps to manage FAW. Three maize fields were planted with imported cultivars, and FAW was monitored using specific pheromone traps to track pest dynamics. Foliar insecticides were applied based on trap data for timely interventions. Results indicated that FAW populations peaked between September 10 and 29, emphasizing the importance of early planting and pre-peak management. The integrated pest management (IPM) approach significantly reduced FAW damage, achieving unobservable infestation levels compared to neighboring farmers using traditional methods. This study underscores the critical role of pheromone traps in monitoring pest populations and reducing insecticide use, providing an effective and sustainable strategy for managing FAW in Lebanese maize fields. Knowledge-sharing activities with neighboring farmers promoted broader adoption of these IPM practices in collaboration with ICARDA and LARI scientists.

title: Pest Management Strategies for Smallholder Farmers in Malawi and Zambia
text: Smallholder farmers in Malawi and Zambia are facing significant challenges to food security due to crop pests and diseases, particularly the fall armyworm (FAW), groundnut rosette virus (GRV), and soybean rust. Approximately 70% of farmers report FAW attacks in maize, 28% experience rosette in groundnuts, and 40% report soybean rust infestations. The impact of these pests is substantial, with yield losses of 13.5% for maize, 27.2% for groundnuts, and 25.2% for soybeans. While FAW negatively affects household income and food security, the combination of FAW with other diseases leads to a greater negative impact. Farmers employ various control strategies, including pesticides, crop rotation, and improved seeds, which have shown some effectiveness in mitigating the adverse effects of these pests. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for developing effective pest management strategies to enhance food security and farmer welfare in the region.

title: Integrated Pest Management Strategies for Cowpea
text: Cowpea is a vital source of protein for many in West Africa, but its annual yields and grain storage longevity are significantly impacted by insect pests. Key pests include pod sucking bugs such as Anoplocnemis curvipes and Clavigralla tomentosicollis, along with phloem-feeding cowpea aphids Aphis craccivora and flower thrips Megalurothrips sjostedti. Controlling these pests poses challenges, necessitating a deeper understanding of their population structure and movement. Molecular tools, including 454 pyrosequencing technology, have been employed to analyze these pests, generating substantial raw reads and assembling numerous transcripts. Functional annotation of these transcripts has revealed genes related to insecticide resistance and immunity, as well as sequences linked to the aphid endosymbiont Buchnera aphidicola. This research underscores the importance of developing integrated pest management strategies to mitigate the impact of these pests on cowpea cultivation.

title: Integrated Pest Management for Cowpea in Semi-arid Southern Africa
text: The importance of multi-dimensional priority-setting for agricultural innovations is increasing, particularly for smallholder farmers in semi-arid southern Africa. This region benefits from agricultural technologies that address multiple roles, including pest management. A promising technology identified in this context is integrated pest management for cowpea, which ranks among the top five technologies for poverty reduction. However, a study utilizing the Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to an Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) indicates that nutrition security is a more pressing concern in this area. Consequently, the top technologies with the highest multi-dimensional impact do not include cowpea but rather focus on pigeon pea, a nutritious grain legume that is more widely consumed in the region. This highlights the need for a comprehensive approach to agricultural technology assessment that considers various outcome criteria, including benefit-cost ratios, poverty reduction, and nutrition security.

title: Integrated Pest and Disease Management for Tomato in Tamil Nadu
text: Tomatoes are a key vegetable crop in Tamil Nadu, India, but their cultivation is challenged by biotic stress, particularly from invasive insect pests and bacterial wilt during the rainy season. Farmers often rely on calendar-based insecticide applications for pest and disease management. However, using resistant tomato hybrids grafted onto bacterial wilt-resistant eggplant rootstocks, such as EG 203, can provide significant protection. Integrated Pest and Disease Management (IPDM) practices include the use of resistant grafted seedlings, bioinoculants like Bacillus subtilis and Trichoderma asperellum, pheromone traps for pests like Phthorimaea absoluta, and microbial pesticides such as Bacillus thuringiensis. Evaluations across four locations in Tamil Nadu showed that the EG 203-grafted tomatoes combined with IPDM practices outperformed other treatments, yielding better results than traditional farmers' practices. This approach not only enhances yield but also promotes sustainable agricultural practices in tomato cultivation.

title: Enhancing Rice Defenses with Soil Silicon
text: Soil silicon has been shown to enhance rice defenses against various biotic stresses, including planthoppers (Nilaparvata lugens and Sogatella furcifera), leafhoppers (Nephotettix virescens), blast disease (Magnaporthe grisea), and bacterial blight (Xanthomonas oryzae). Greenhouse experiments revealed that adding powdered silica gel (SiO2) to paddy soil at rates of 0.25, 1.0, and 4.0 t ha−1 significantly reduced BPH nymph settling and egg-laying, particularly in susceptible rice varieties. However, the effects were less pronounced under high nitrogen conditions. Silicon also reduced blast damage in both susceptible and resistant rice varieties. While it decreased damage from a virulent strain of bacterial blight, its impact was minimal on a less virulent strain. When combined with host resistance, silicon demonstrated an additive effect in reducing biomass losses from bacterial blight. This suggests that silicon-containing soil amendments can be effectively integrated with host resistance strategies to manage pests and diseases in rice cultivation.

title: Assessing low soil organic matter
text: Diagnosing low soil organic matter. Look for pale, hard-setting soil that crusts after rain and dries fast; a simple test is poor crumb structure and low earthworm activity.

title: Low soil organic matter: the problem
text: Low soil organic matter in smallholder farming. Soils low in organic matter hold little water and few nutrients, crust over, and lose structure, so seedlings struggle and fertiliser is wasted.

title: Managing low soil organic matter (Guinea savanna)
text: Managing low soil organic matter in the Guinea savanna, with one long rainy season and moderately fertile soils. Add compost and well-rotted manure, return crop residues, grow cover crops and green manures, and minimise burning and excessive tillage. In the Guinea savanna, time operations to the single rains, top-dress at the onset of steady rainfall, and use the long season for a full-duration variety.

title: Assessing soil acidity
text: Diagnosing soil acidity. Test pH with a meter or kit; below about 5.5 most cereals and legumes suffer. Watch for stunted purple-tinged plants and poor nodulation.

title: Soil acidity: the problem
text: Soil acidity in smallholder farming. Strongly acidic soils (low pH) lock up phosphorus, free toxic aluminium and manganese, and stunt roots, so crops respond poorly to fertiliser.

title: Managing soil acidity (Guinea savanna)
text: Managing soil acidity in the Guinea savanna, with one long rainy season and moderately fertile soils. Apply agricultural lime (or dolomitic lime where magnesium is low) several weeks before planting, build organic matter, and choose acid-tolerant varieties. In the Guinea savanna, time operations to the single rains, top-dress at the onset of steady rainfall, and use the long season for a full-duration variety.

title: Assessing soil compaction
text: Diagnosing soil compaction. Probe for a hard layer, watch for shallow flattened roots, water ponding, and stunted patches on trafficked ground.

title: Soil compaction: the problem
text: Soil compaction in smallholder farming. A hard compacted layer (hardpan) from tillage or traffic blocks roots and water, causing waterlogging above and drought stress below.

title: Managing soil compaction (Guinea savanna)
text: Managing soil compaction in the Guinea savanna, with one long rainy season and moderately fertile soils. title: Enhancing Maize Yields through Agroecological Practices in Makueni County
text: Agroecology is a sustainable approach that can transform food systems in low and middle-income countries, particularly in improving soil and crop productivity. A study conducted in Makueni County, Kenya, assessed the impact of innovative agroecology practices on maize and bean crops in nutrient deficient sandy soils. The practices tested included the use of biopesticides (IPM), terracing, and organic inputs (manure). Results indicated that the combined use of biopesticides and organic inputs significantly increased maize yields compared to other practices. Specifically, maize yields rose by 109 kilograms per acre under terracing, 78 kilograms under manure, and 40 kilograms under IPM, leading to monetary gains of USD$ 50.26, 36.14, and 18.28 per acre, respectively. Additionally, bean yields also improved, with increases of 20.7 kilograms under IPM, 33.3 kilograms under manure, and 19.8 kilograms under terraces. These findings underscore the importance of agroecological practices in enhancing crop productivity and soil health.

title: Economic and Environmental Viability of Liming Acid Soils for Maize in Western Kenya
text: Soil acidification negatively impacts crop yields, which can reduce farmers' incomes. While lime application can increase soil pH, its economic viability is crucial, particularly for smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa who often face short-term decision-making challenges. Liming is a long-term investment, with benefits manifesting over several years. This study assessed the economic and environmental viability of liming acid soils for maize cultivation in Western Kenya. A meta-analysis of 26 field experiments was conducted to evaluate the effects of lime on soil pH and maize yields, alongside estimating farm profits and returns on investment over five years. The results indicated that liming consistently enhanced maize yields in soils with an initial pH between 4.0 and 5.7, regardless of fertiliser use. However, the application of lime is associated with significant greenhouse gas emissions, particularly CO2, raising questions about its overall environmental impact when crop yields increase.

title: Addressing Soil Acidity in Sub-Saharan Africa
text: Soil acidity has become a significant agricultural productivity constraint in several Sub-Saharan African countries, particularly in Tanzania. Despite the known agronomic benefits of using agricultural lime to mitigate soil acidity, its adoption among farmers remains limited. The development of value chains for agricultural lime is also underdeveloped in many acidic regions. Policymakers are exploring various strategies, such as targeted extension services, investments in lime production, and market development, to enhance lime usage. However, they face challenges due to insufficient evidence regarding farmers' valuation of lime and their demand dynamics. A study conducted in Iringa District, Tanzania, involving 600 randomly selected farm households, estimated the mean willingness to pay for lime at 4.67 US dollars per 50-kilogram bag, which aligns with market prices. Notably, the willingness to pay varies among farmers, with social exposure—specifically, the number of known lime users—being a strong predictor of demand. This highlights the importance of social networks in influencing agricultural practices.

title: Addressing Soil Acidity in Ethiopia
text: Soil acidity is a significant challenge for agricultural production in Ethiopia, affecting over 43% of farmland and resulting in low crop yields and production losses. Ag-lime is recognized as an effective solution for amending soil acidity. A study focusing on the ag-lime value chain in central Ethiopia reveals that both public and private ag-lime producing factories are operating below capacity, with minimal engagement from the private sector due to limited enabling environments. While farmers are generally aware of the soil acidity problem and its causes, the adoption of ag-lime among smallholders remains low. The ag-lime value chain is currently fragmented and requires improvement. Enhancing the efficiency of this value chain could help address the soil acidity challenge, reduce lime supply-demand mismatches, and promote wider adoption of ag-lime by farmers, ultimately improving crop productivity and food security in acidity-prone regions of the country.

title: Liming for Soil Acidity Management in Highland Barley Production
text: Soil acidity is a significant constraint for crop production in the highlands of Ethiopia. A study conducted from 2020 to 2021 on acidic Nitisols (pH < 5.5) evaluated the effects of liming at six different rates (control, 2.74, 4.11, 5.48, 6.85, and 8.22 t·ha−1). Results showed that lime application increased soil pH by 0.46–1.25 units and reduced exchangeable acidity by 2.02–3.17 units. Notably, higher lime rates (6.85–8.22 t·ha−1) significantly raised soil pH but did not proportionally increase crop yield. The optimal lime application rate of 5.45 t·ha−1 resulted in the highest barley total biomass of 19,199 kg·ha−1 and a grain yield of 4,328 kg·ha−1, which were 46% and 30% higher than the control, respectively. This rate also provided a marginal rate of return of 477% and a gross margin of 192,857.3 ETB·ha−1, indicating its economic viability for barley production.

title: Addressing Soil Acidity for Wheat Production in Ethiopia
text: Soil acidity is a significant constraint to crop production in Ethiopia, particularly affecting wheat-based mixed farming systems. It leads to poor soil health, inefficient fertilizer use, substantial crop yield losses, and a shortage of livestock feed. The variability of soil acidity levels across the country necessitates context-specific lime recommendations. A study identified six acid saturation models, two target pH models, and one base saturation model to develop site-specific lime requirements for acid-affected areas. Among these, the modified Kamprath model, the LiTAS model, and a target pH model were parameterized for wheat on acid soils. The lime requirements derived from these models ranged from 0-1.8 tons per hectare for the modified Kamprath model, 0-3.2 tons per hectare for the target pH model, and 0-22 tons per hectare for the LiTAS model over four growing seasons. Expert validation confirmed the effectiveness of these models in ameliorating acid soils for improved wheat production.

title: Impact of Soil Acidity on Soybean Production in Southwestern Ethiopia
text: Soil acidity, coupled with low nutrient availability, significantly constrains soybean production in southwestern Ethiopia. An experiment conducted during the 2017/18 cropping season in Mettu evaluated fifteen soybean genotypes under two soil amendment treatments: lime-treated and unlimed soils. The study utilized a split-plot design with three replications, planting four rows per plot. Results indicated that liming and genotype interactions significantly affected growth, root, nodule, and yield parameters, with the exception of hundred seed weight and root volume. Most parameters showed a significant reduction in lime-untreated soils compared to treated soils. Although some genotypes performed better in unlimed conditions, overall yield was higher in lime-treated soils, with an average yield reduction of 13.7% due to soil acidity. The highest grain yield of 1943.93 kg ha-1 was recorded from the PI567046A genotype in lime-treated soil, while the lowest yield of 510.49 kg ha-1 was from the SCS-1 genotype in unlimed soil.

title: Managing Soil Acidity for Improved Maize Production in Southwestern Oromia
text: Soil acidity significantly hampers crop production in tropical regions, particularly in the highlands of Southwestern Oromia, Ethiopia, where maize is a key crop. This study assessed the impact of soil amendments and phosphorus (P) fertilization on soil properties, maize physiology, and grain yield over the 2023 and 2024 growing seasons across 14 farmers' fields. A split-plot design was employed, testing four soil amendments (control, calcitic lime, biochar, vermicompost) and four P rates (0, 15, 30, and 45 kg P ha⁻¹). Results indicated that calcitic lime and vermicompost significantly enhanced soil fertility, improved maize performance, and increased yields, with lime being particularly effective in raising soil pH and reducing acidity saturation. Yield gains ranged from 38–78% with lime and 41–66% with vermicompost compared to the control. While P fertilization boosted yields, its effectiveness diminished under high acidity conditions. Thus, addressing soil acidity is crucial for maximizing maize productivity in these regions.

title: Integrated Soil Fertility Management for Smallholder Agriculture
text: Intensification of smallholder agriculture in sub-Saharan Africa is essential to combat rural poverty and natural resource degradation. Integrated Soil Fertility Management (ISFM) enhances crop productivity and agronomic efficiency (AE) through a combination of best practices. These practices include the use of suitable germplasm, appropriate fertilizer and organic resource application, and sound agronomic techniques. ISFM acknowledges the variability in soil fertility conditions on smallholder farms, which may have constraints beyond what fertilizers and organic inputs can address. title: Addressing Soil Health Decline in Southern and Eastern Africa
text: In Southern and Eastern Africa, input subsidy programmes focusing on inorganic fertiliser often fail to meet food security objectives due to declining soil health. This decline is attributed to years of inorganic fertiliser application without complementary soil improvement measures. Solutions to enhance soil health are well established and include practices such as fallowing, crop diversification, intercropping, crop rotations (especially with legumes), adding organic matter, liming, and applying suitable inorganic fertilisers. However, these solutions present significant socio-economic and technical challenges for farmers. A promising approach is to compensate farmers for providing soil health services, which can yield numerous private and public benefits. This concept aligns with the Payment for Environmental Services (PES) framework, supported by the global initiative CompensACTION. To implement soil health payment schemes effectively, development partners can assist by establishing pilot schemes for learning, supporting long-term soil health monitoring, helping to repurpose subsidy policies, and facilitating public-private partnerships to attract private sector investment.
